Review Finds Early Childhood Classrooms Have Yet to Fully Integrate Artificial Intelligence

In a comprehensive review published in AI, Brain and Child, researcher Jennifer J. Chen examined the historical development and modern applications of artificial intelligence in early childhood education. Synthesizing literature on educational practices serving children from birth to age eight, the review concluded that while the educational sector has initiated a paradigm shift toward AI adoption, classrooms have yet to achieve full integration of these technologies.

The analysis evaluated conceptual, empirical, and practical perspectives across nearly eight decades of machine intelligence history. Published in February 2025, the study generated and analyzed no original datasets, relying instead on a systematic synthesis of existing academic literature to assess developmental, instructional, and ethical dimensions of artificial intelligence in early childhood settings.

Chen situated contemporary educational tools within a broader historical context, tracing the origins of computational concepts back to Alan Turing’s 1947 formulation of machine intelligence. The review also highlighted the formal introduction of the term artificial intelligence by John McCarthy and colleagues in 1955, noting how these early theoretical foundations eventually catalyzed a global expansion of applied computational tools.

Over the past two decades, computational technologies have increasingly altered how people communicate, interact, teach, and learn. Within early childhood education specifically, researchers during this period have focused primarily on cataloging available artificial intelligence tools and examining how these tools can support different domains of children’s learning and development.

Despite growing interest in deploying artificial intelligence to create more engaging and personalized learning experiences, the review found that classroom adoption remains incomplete.

Ethical considerations and developmental appropriateness form central pillars of Chen’s framework.

The synthesis identified emerging opportunities alongside pedagogical challenges for educators working with children up to age eight. To navigate these issues, the review recommended that early childhood teachers cultivate positive dispositions, including open-mindedness, adaptability, and instructional integrity, while engaging directly with evolving digital systems.

Educational leadership also plays a critical role in facilitating responsible technology adoption.

Looking toward future classroom environments, the review envisioned interactive educational spaces featuring smart robots and adaptive digital platforms. In these settings, children could interact with robotic tools by learning from them and teaching them, while adaptive platforms provide personalized instruction across diverse academic and developmental domains.

The review concluded that realizing a transformative educational landscape requires equitable resources and equal access for all children. By ensuring that young learners can engage naturally with developmentally sound artificial intelligence tools, educators, families, and policymakers can collaboratively support constructive technology use across early childhood education.

The review documents how computational innovations have begun permeating everyday society, demonstrating substantial transformative potential for instructional delivery and student learning.

The author situates current educational technologies within a historical progression spanning nearly eight decades of computational theory and design. Chen traces the conceptual foundations of automated cognition to Alan Turing’s 1947 formulation of machine intelligence, followed by the formal naming of artificial intelligence by John McCarthy and colleagues in 1955. The review explains that these theoretical breakthroughs ultimately catalyzed the contemporary global phenomenon of widespread knowledge, investigation, and practical application of digital systems.

Examining more recent history, the synthesis underscores that the past two decades have witnessed artificial intelligence steadily altering how individuals live, communicate, interact, teach, and learn. Within early childhood education specifically, academic inquiry over this period has concentrated predominantly on cataloging existing computational instruments and evaluating how these tools support various developmental and learning areas. Chen notes that children are being educated in an increasingly technology-propelled world where computational advancements continually influence educational environments.

To keep pace with rapid technological advancements, the educational sector has initiated a notable paradigm shift toward incorporating artificial intelligence within early childhood education. Citing foundational scholarship from researchers including Chen and Perez, Su and colleagues, Su and Yang, Su and Zhong, as well as Vartiainen and collaborators, the review demonstrates that this emerging shift aims to make children’s educational experiences significantly more engaging, dynamic, and personalized. Nevertheless, Chen emphasizes that contemporary early childhood education has yet to accomplish complete integration within everyday classroom settings.

A central dimension of the review focuses on categorizing the practical applications of artificial intelligence within early childhood education across three distinct modalities: technologies utilized by children, technologies designed for children, and technologies implemented with children. Chen stresses that across all three operational modalities, developmental appropriateness and ethical considerations must remain paramount.

To characterize the unpredictable trajectory of emerging educational technology, Chen invokes the perspective of Yoda, the fictional humanoid alien character and legendary Jedi master in the Star Wars films. Highlighting the character’s hyperbaton phrasing that the future is difficult to see and always in motion, the author emphasizes the dynamic, constantly shifting, and uncertain nature of technological evolution, which remains subject to many complex factors. Despite this inherent unpredictability, Chen asserts that artificial intelligence remains a remarkably powerful force.

Navigating this evolving landscape requires sustained collaboration among all primary stakeholders in children’s education, explicitly including classroom educators, educational administrators, families, and policymakers. Chen argues that these key groups must actively keep pace with emerging technological developments by navigating new instructional opportunities while proactively addressing emerging challenges. The review emphasizes the essential necessity of cultivating supportive practices, active engagement, and positive dispositions across every stakeholder group. In particular, the author highlights open-mindedness, adaptable responsiveness, professional integrity, and creative ingenuity as indispensable dispositions. By maintaining these shared qualities, educational leaders and teachers can ensure that ethical considerations and developmental appropriateness remain central to ongoing institutional integration efforts.

Visualizing future classroom environments, Chen envisions an educational space bustling with discovery, active curiosity, and intellectual excitement, where children interact with advanced digital tools in deeply enriching ways. In this progressive setting, young learners participate in bi-directional learning relationships, actively interacting with smart robots to both acquire knowledge from the machines and teach them through guided activities. Furthermore, the review highlights the integration of adaptive educational platforms capable of delivering personalized instructional support across multiple academic and developmental domains.
